solution:
The chapter gives two figures in consecutive sentences: "The 73rd and 74th amendment reserved 33% of seats for women in local self-governing institutions. This percentage has been raised to 50% in several states including Maharashtra." The question asks specifically about Maharashtra, so the answer is (d) 50%.

The trap is 30%, which is roughly the national figure from the 73rd and 74th amendments — but the chapter gives that figure as 33%, not 30%, and then explicitly raises it for Maharashtra. Neither 25% nor 40% appears anywhere in the chapter.

The chapter lists the measures together: "The right to have an equal share in the property of the father and husband, Dowry Prohibition Act, act against sexual harassment, Domestic Violence Prohibition Act are some important provisions which create a favourable environment for protection of freedom of women and securing their development." The question's wording is a compression of that same clause, and the Dowry Prohibition Act is the only item from the list that appears among the options, so the answer is (b).

The chapter presents the Right to Information as a general transparency measure for all citizens rather than a women-specific one, and mentions food security only in its list of citizens' rights. Since option (b) is drawn straight from the chapter's own list, 'None of the above' is ruled out.

The chapter makes exactly one statement of this form: "Decentralisation of power is central to democratic government. Decentralisation controls the misuse of power and also creates opportunities for political participation for the common people." So the answer is (b) decentralisation of power.

The four options match the chapter's four section headings, and only this one carries a 'central to' claim. Universal adult franchise is the option worth pausing on, because outside the textbook it is a very common way to describe the essence of democracy — but this chapter presents adult suffrage as a constitutional provision and an achievement (it is what makes India the largest democracy in the world), never as democracy's essence. Reservation of seats is described as a remedial measure for sections of society deprived of opportunities, and judicial decisions are described as strengthening democracy rather than constituting it.

[Note: the chapter's one use of the word 'essence' is in a different sentence — "The essence of representative system is to integrate the principles of democracy in actual practice" — whose predicate matches none of the printed options.]
